title: 7. Why the Price Is What It Is: Valuation, Reverse DCF & Peer Comps

epigraph.quote: When a software transformation is still priced like a cyclical print shop, the valuation gap closes only as fast as the recurring mix proves its durability.
epigraph.author: Institutional Research Desk

web_blocks.html: At the November 16, 2026 close of $70.06, DFIN carries a $1.71 billion market cap (24.50 million shares; 22.75 million float) and a $1.81 billion enterprise value (EV) [30]. Shares trade at 18.47x trailing GAAP P/E ($3.79 TTM EPS) and 12.41x forward P/E (~$5.65 forward EPS) [30]. That implies a 0.94 PEG ratio on 13.22% projected five-year EPS growth [30]. On cash flow and sales, DFIN trades at 8.06x EV/EBITDA, 2.30x EV/Sales, 2.17x Price/Sales, and 4.20x Price/Book [30]. Price/FCF sits at 9.54x after Q3 2026's $85.8 million FCF surge, or ~15.9x on normalized FY2025 FCF of $107.8 million [15, 30, 42]. This valuation sits just below the $75.33 sell-side target after a 45.47% three-month rally [30].

Why does DFIN trade at 8.06x EV/EBITDA and 12.41x forward earnings despite 18.25% ROIC, 23.41% ROE, and 51.5% Q3 2026 software mix [11, 30]? A Reverse DCF model shows what the market expects. We start with a $1.81 billion EV, $787.2 million trailing sales, a 9.5% WACC (0.69 beta, 0.33x debt-to-equity, small-cap size), and a 2.5% terminal growth rate [30]. At $70.06, the market prices in only 3.5% to 4.5% annual sales growth over the next decade. It assumes normalized FCF margins stay near 14.5% to 15.5%, starting at ~$115 million to $130 million and reaching ~$180 million by Year 10 [15, 30]. In plain terms, investors credit DFIN for holding >30% Adjusted EBITDA margins. Yet they do NOT price in faster top-line growth or pure-play SaaS multiples.

A Sum-of-the-Parts (SOTP) model shows this gap better than one blended multiple. DFIN runs two very different units under one ticker. First, Software Solutions (ActiveDisclosure, Arc Suite, and Venue VDR) posted $358.4 million in FY2025 sales and hit 51.5% of net sales in Q3 2026 ($95.2 million quarterly) [10, 11]. That implies a ~$385 million FY2026 run-rate and ~$420 million in FY2027E on ~9% blended growth, led by ActiveDisclosure at +24% YoY [10, 11]. Second, Compliance & Communications Management (CM-CCM and IC-CCM) posted $408.6 million in FY2025 [10]. Due to print runoff and IPO/M&A swings, we model CCM conservatively at ~$380 million in FY2027E [10, 15].

web_blocks.takeaway: DFIN trades at 8.06x EV/EBITDA and 9.54x P/FCF with an industry-leading 18.25% ROIC, representing a steep valuation discount to Broadridge (14.07x EV/EBITDA, 17.06% ROIC) and Workiva (57.06x EV/EBITDA, 9.46% ROIC) due to its legacy print tail and smaller $1.71B market cap [30].

web_blocks.html: Comparing DFIN against its three closest peers clarifies both the upside and the discount [30, 35]. Workiva (WK, $3.69B market cap) is DFIN's main rival in SEC reporting and ActiveDisclosure workflows [35]. Workiva grows sales faster (+18.80% YoY vs. DFIN's +4.85% TTM) and trades at 3.68x P/S and 19.54x forward P/E [30]. Yet Workiva earns just a 5.25% operating margin and 9.46% ROIC, trading at 57.06x EV/EBITDA [30]. Broadridge (BR, $22.08B market cap) shares DFIN's focus on fund and proxy filings. Broadridge posts 17.06% ROIC and 17.17% operating margins—below DFIN's 18.25% ROIC and 20.33% margin [30]. Even so, Broadridge commands 14.07x EV/EBITDA and 16.88x forward P/E due to its larger recurring fee base [30]. Finally, SS&C Technologies (SSNC, $18.68B market cap) trades at 9.76x EV/EBITDA and 10.25x forward P/E with 24.50% operating margins, though higher debt and 6.05% ROIC weigh on quality [30].

Past valuation cycles show that 8.06x EV/EBITDA and 12.41x forward P/E sit well below normal software-majority levels [30]. During the 2021 SPAC and IPO boom ($993.3 million sales, $219.3 million GAAP operating income), investors viewed DFIN's earnings as temporary windfalls [8, 14]. During the 2022–2024 deal freeze, they feared print runoff would overwhelm software growth [8, 15]. In Q3 2026, Software Solutions crossed 51.5% of sales while Adjusted EBITDA margins held near 30%+ [11, 15]. Each quarter of 20%+ ActiveDisclosure growth and steady share buybacks should narrow the gap toward Broadridge (14.07x) and SS&C (9.76x) [11, 30, 40].

web_blocks.the_number: $92.00 per share (12–18 Month SOTP Base Fair Value; +31.3% vs. $70.06 CMP, +42.5% vs. $64.55 support)
web_blocks.how_calculated: Software EV is $1,785M (4.25x FY27E $420M sales). CCM EV is $475M (5.0x $95M EBITDA). Subtract $60M corporate drag for $2,200M EV, then subtract $65M net debt for $2,135M equity across 23.2M shares.
web_blocks.the_inputs: FY27E Software sales $420M (+9% YoY); CCM EBITDA $95M (~25% margin on $380M); FY25 net debt $146.8M cut by ~$110M+ FCF; 24.50M shares reduced via $150M buyback plan [15, 30, 40].
web_blocks.the_range: $52.00 Bear (6.0x EBITDA on IPO/M&A freeze) to $110.00 Bull (5.0x Software EV/Sales + 6.0x CCM EBITDA).
web_blocks.if_off: If ActiveDisclosure growth falls below 12% YoY or print drops >10% yearly, SOTP fair value falls toward $70–$75. That would erase the 1.50:1 support-zone edge.

web_blocks.title: Why the Discount Persists — And What Closes It
paragraphs: 1. The 'Print & Deal-Cycle' Discount: CCM and Venue rooms still make up nearly half of sales. Screeners penalize DFIN's +3.4% 9M 2026 sales growth versus pure-play SaaS peers [17, 30].

2. Multiple Re-Rating Catalyst: Crossing 51.5% software mix in Q3 2026 sparked DFIN's 35.5% one-month rally [11, 30]. Sustained 20%+ ActiveDisclosure growth and an IPO/M&A rebound can lift EBITDA toward $260M+ and push EV/EBITDA to 9.0x–9.5x toward $92.00 [11, 30].

web_blocks.html: Valuation Re-Rating Trigger: Our $92.00 SOTP base target moves down toward $70–$75 if ActiveDisclosure growth slows below 12% YoY or CCM print declines exceed 10% annually; conversely, Software Solutions scaling past 55% of sales alongside a rebound in US IPO/M&A filings supports re-rating toward $110.00 (5.0x Software EV/Sales).

book_paragraphs: Now that we have spent six chapters auditing Donnelley Financial Solutions without looking at its stock chart or valuation multiple, it is time to open the price tape and ask the central question of investing: why does the market price DFIN at $70.06 per share, and what future is baked into that tag?

Let's put the exact numbers on the table as of the November 16, 2026 close. At $70.06, DFIN carries an equity market capitalization of $1.71 billion across 24.50 million shares, and an enterprise value of $1.81 billion. On trailing numbers, the stock trades at 18.47 times GAAP earnings, 8.06 times EV-to-EBITDA, 2.17 times sales, and 9.54 times trailing free cash flow—a figure boosted by a massive $85.8 million cash-flow surge in the third quarter of 2026. Look one year forward, and DFIN trades at just 12.41 times forward earnings, with a PEG ratio of 0.94 against 13.22% projected five-year earnings growth.

Wait a minute. Stop and think about that mismatch. You and I just verified that DFIN generates an 18.25% return on invested capital, a 23.41% return on equity, and a 20.33% operating margin, with Software Solutions now generating more than half of quarterly revenue. Why would a software-majority business with nearly 20% ROIC trade at 12.4 times forward earnings and 8 times EBITDA when the average mid-cap software company trades at double or triple those multiples?

To answer that honestly, let's run two valuation lenses: a Reverse Discounted Cash Flow model to see what the market is already pricing in, and a Sum-of-the-Parts valuation to see what the two halves of DFIN are worth on their own.

Start with the Reverse DCF. When you plug DFIN's $1.81 billion enterprise value into a standard ten-year cash-flow model using a 9.5% discount rate—appropriate for a $1.7 billion small-cap with low leverage and a 0.69 beta—and a 2.5% terminal growth rate, you discover what the market believes. To justify $70.06, DFIN only needs to grow consolidated revenue at about 3.5% to 4.5% a year while maintaining normalized free cash flow margins around 14.5% to 15.5%. That means starting around $115 million to $130 million in normalized annual free cash flow and compounding slowly toward $180 million a decade out. In other words, Wall Street is giving Daniel Leib credit for keeping margins above 30% Adjusted EBITDA, but it is assuming that legacy print shrinkage will keep consolidated growth stuck in low gear forever.

Now flip the lens to a Sum-of-the-Parts breakdown, because blending a high-margin cloud SaaS business with a shrinking print business under one consolidated multiple hides the real economics. Suppose we look ahead 12 to 18 months to fiscal 2027. On the software side, Software Solutions did $358.4 million in 2025 and crossed 51.5% of sales in Q3 2026. Growing at a blended 9% pace—with ActiveDisclosure compounding above 20% and Arc Suite in the mid-teens—Software Solutions reaches roughly $420 million in 2027 revenue. What is a sticky, regulated, >30% EBITDA-margin compliance SaaS franchise worth?

Look right next door at Workiva, ticker WK, DFIN's direct rival in SEC reporting. Workiva grows faster at 18.8% year-over-year, and the market values Workiva at 3.68 times sales, 19.5 times forward earnings, and 57 times EV-to-EBITDA—even though Workiva only earns a 5.25% operating margin and a 9.46% return on invested capital. If we value DFIN's far more profitable Software Solutions segment at a conservative 4.25 times 2027 sales, that single segment alone is worth $1.785 billion in enterprise value—nearly the entire $1.81 billion enterprise value of the whole company today.

And what about the other half, Compliance and Communications Management? Even if you model print runoff continuing at 4% to 5% a year, taking CCM revenue from $408.6 million in 2025 down toward $380 million in 2027, that segment still throws off roughly $95 million in annual EBITDA. Put a deeply discounted, melting-ice-cube multiple of just 5.0 times EBITDA on CCM, and it adds another $475 million of enterprise value. Subtract $60 million for unallocated corporate overhead, and you arrive at a base-case Sum-of-the-Parts enterprise value of $2.20 billion.

Now follow the capital-allocation math to the per-share price. DFIN ended 2025 with $146.8 million in net debt, and it is generating over $100 million a year in free cash flow while actively buying back stock under its $150 million authorization. By 2027, net debt can easily step down toward $65 million while the diluted share count shrinks toward 23.2 million shares. Divide $2.135 billion of implied equity value by 23.2 million shares, and you get a base-case fair value of roughly $92.00 per share—about 31% above today's close.

What if we stress-test that math? Suppose you are even more skeptical and value Software Solutions at just 3.5 times sales and legacy print at 4.0 times EBITDA. Even under that harsher multiple assumption, the Sum-of-the-Parts value lands around $74.35 per share—still above today's $70.06 price. Conversely, if ActiveDisclosure accelerates and capital markets thaw enough for Software Solutions to earn 5.0 times sales alongside 6.0 times EBITDA for CCM, fair value stretches toward $110.00 per share.

Let's also sanity-check that against DFIN's other two public peers: Broadridge Financial Solutions, ticker BR, and SS&C Technologies, ticker SSNC. Broadridge is a $22 billion powerhouse in fund communications and proxy processing. Broadridge earns a 17.06% ROIC and a 17.17% operating margin—both slightly lower than DFIN's 18.25% ROIC and 20.33% operating margin—yet Broadridge trades at 14.07 times EV-to-EBITDA and 16.88 times forward earnings. Why? Because Broadridge has scale and minimal transactional IPO volatility. Meanwhile, SS&C Technologies trades at 9.76 times EV-to-EBITDA and 10.25 times forward earnings, with a 24.50% operating margin but much lower ROIC of 6.05% due to acquisition goodwill.

So why does DFIN still trade at 8.06 times EV-to-EBITDA instead of 10 or 12 times? Three honest reasons. First, legacy print is still shrinking, which drags down consolidated revenue growth to around 3.4% to 4.9% and keeps pure-play software funds away. Second, Venue Virtual Data Rooms and capital-markets filings remain tied to IPO and M&A deal cycles, creating quarterly lumpiness. Third, at $1.71 billion in market cap, DFIN is a small-cap Russell 2000 name with thinner sell-side coverage. In fact, after surging 35.5% in a single month, the stock at $70.06 has nearly caught up to the $75.33 Wall Street consensus target.

Think about the psychology of that moment. For three years, DFIN sat in the penalty box because investors saw flat-to-down consolidated revenue and assumed it was a melting print business. Then Q3 2026 hit, Software Solutions crossed 51.5% of total sales, and quarterly free cash flow surged to $85.8 million. Overnight, generalist investors woke up to the software mix shift and bid the stock up 45% in three months. That re-rating took DFIN from deeply overlooked to fairly recognized in the short term—while still leaving substantial medium-term upside toward $92.00 as the software majority compounds.

The takeaway from Chapter 7 is straightforward: DFIN is genuinely undervalued on a Sum-of-the-Parts and through-cycle cash-flow basis, with a defensible 12-to-18-month base value near $92.00 if software continues compounding and net debt falls. But as we are about to see in Chapter 8, a cheap long-term business and a safe short-term entry point are two very different things.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION: The Sum-of-the-Parts Arbitrage
book_callouts.text: When a company's growing software division ($1.785B at 4.25x sales) is worth almost the entire enterprise value ($1.81B) of the consolidated firm, you are effectively getting a $95M-EBITDA legacy cash-cow segment for free. The catch is that closing that gap takes patience—and buying after a 45% three-month spike violates entry discipline.

book_subsections.title: 7A. Walking Through the Reverse DCF Math Step by Step
paragraphs: Whenever you hear an analyst say a stock is 'cheap' or 'expensive,' your first follow-up question should always be: compared to what cash-flow expectations? A Reverse Discounted Cash Flow model strips away guesswork by starting with today's actual $1.81 billion enterprise value and solving backward for the growth and margin assumptions required to earn a fair 9.5% annual return.

Here is how that arithmetic works for DFIN. Trailing twelve-month sales stand at $787.2 million, and normalized free cash flow—stripping out working-capital timing spikes—runs around $108 million to $120 million, or roughly 14% to 15% of revenue. If you assume DFIN's capital structure stays conservative with net debt near $100 million and a 0.69 beta, a 9.5% weighted average cost of capital and a 2.5% terminal growth rate are standard institutional inputs.

Under those parameters, $1.81 billion of enterprise value requires DFIN to compound consolidated revenue at just 3.5% to 4.5% per year over the next decade while holding free cash flow margins in the 14.5% to 15.5% band. Notice what is missing from that market-implied forecast: zero credit for Software Solutions expanding consolidated margins toward 33% or 35% Adjusted EBITDA as print shrinks, and zero credit for share count shrinking from 24.5 million toward 22 million via buybacks. That is why the market's implied bar is surprisingly low—even after a 45% three-month rally.

book_subsections.title: 7B. Why Small-Cap Hybrid Transitions Trade at a Discount Until Inflection
paragraphs: If the Reverse DCF bar is so low and Sum-of-the-Parts points to $92.00, why did DFIN spend years trading at 6 to 8 times EBITDA? The answer lies in institutional mandate silos. Pure-play enterprise software funds screen for 15% to 20% consolidated revenue growth and 75% gross margins; DFIN's 57.14% gross margin and 3.4% to 4.9% consolidated top-line growth disqualify it from their universe. Meanwhile, deep-value industrial investors see a $1.7 billion former R.R. Donnelley print spin-off with 4.20x price-to-book and look elsewhere.

DFIN sits in the valuation no-man's-land between those two camps. Historically, hybrid transitions only close that conglomerate discount when two things happen together: first, the recurring software segment crosses 50% of total sales—which DFIN just achieved in Q3 2026 at 51.5%—and second, consolidated revenue growth accelerates into the mid-to-high single digits as print runoff becomes a smaller denominator. Once ActiveDisclosure ($100 million+ TTM, +24% YoY) and Arc Suite push Software Solutions toward 55% to 60% of sales in 2027, generalist mid-cap growth-at-a-reasonable-price funds can finally own the name without apologizing for the print tail.

book_subsections.title: 7C. Historical Multiple Cycles & What Rerates DFIN to 9.5x–10.5x EBITDA
paragraphs: Looking back across DFIN's ten-year public history, the stock has never enjoyed a sustained pure-play software multiple because investors kept waiting for the other shoe to drop. During the 2021 SPAC and IPO boom, when revenue hit $993.3 million and operating income surged to $219.3 million, Wall Street rightly discounted those earnings as peak-cycle windfalls. Then during the 2022–2024 IPO drought, when consolidated sales drifted down to $781.9 million, skeptics worried that shrinking physical print would eventually drag down margins.

What changed in 2025 and 2026 is proof of structural permanence. Even without a 2021-style SPAC mania, DFIN delivered a record 31.3% Adjusted EBITDA margin in 2025 and generated $167.3 million in operating cash flow through the first nine months of 2026. When a company proves it can earn 30%+ EBITDA margins in a normal-to-sluggish deal environment while software grows to 51.5% of the pie, the old cyclical ceiling gives way. You do not need DFIN to trade at Workiva's 57 times EBITDA or Broadridge's 14 times EBITDA to make money; a simple re-rating from 8.06 times EV-to-EBITDA to 8.6 or 9.5 times on $255 million to $275 million of 2027 EBITDA—paired with steady share buybacks—bridges the path to $92.00 in our Base Case and $110.00 in our Bull Case.

book_subsections.title: 7D. Free Cash Flow Yield, Buybacks, and Per-Share Compounding Math
paragraphs: There is one final piece of valuation math that often gets overlooked when investors focus only on EV-to-EBITDA: per-share free cash flow compounding through share repurchases. DFIN ended 2025 with roughly 24.50 million shares outstanding, down meaningfully since its 2016 spin-off, and management backed that discipline with a $150 million share repurchase authorization in May 2025—retiring more than 787,000 shares in a single quarter.

Think about what happens when a $1.71 billion company generates $108 million to $130 million in normalized annual free cash flow with net leverage already down around 0.6 times EBITDA and its legacy pension plan settled. After funding $57 million to $60 million in capitalized software development, DFIN has almost $100 million a year of excess cash flow to split between modest debt paydown and retiring roughly 3% to 5% of its share count annually. Even if revenue only grows 4% to 5% and EBITDA margins hold steady, retiring 4% of shares each year turns mid-single-digit operating growth into double-digit free cash flow per share growth—which is why the 0.94 PEG ratio on 13.22% projected five-year EPS growth makes complete mathematical sense.

Put all four valuation lenses together—the Reverse DCF showing only 3.5% to 4.5% implied top-line growth, the Sum-of-the-Parts yielding $92.03 at 4.25 times Software sales and 5.0 times CCM EBITDA, the peer comparison showing DFIN's 18.25% ROIC trading at half Broadridge's EV-to-EBITDA multiple, and the 4% annual share-count shrink from buybacks—and the valuation conclusion is rock solid. At $70.06, DFIN is not expensive on intrinsic value; it is simply extended on the short-term price chart.

book_subsections.title: 7E. What Consensus Street Targets Miss After a Rapid Re-Rating
paragraphs: One question listeners often ask is why the published Wall Street consensus price target sits at $75.33—barely 7.5% above the $70.06 close—if our Sum-of-the-Parts model points to $92.00. The answer is mechanical lag. Sell-side analysts covering a $1.71 billion small-cap update their models quarterly, not daily. When DFIN surged 35.54% in a single month after Q3 2026 earnings, the stock price sprinted right up to old Street targets that were anchored on 2025 trough multiples.

As analysts roll their valuation models forward into FY2027 and begin valuing Software Solutions as the majority (>51.5%) revenue engine rather than a secondary division, consensus targets typically step higher in waves. Still, you never want to buy a stock solely because Street targets might catch up; you want to buy when the price gives you a clear margin of safety against your own downside.

In fact, that gap between lagging Street targets and forward Sum-of-the-Parts value is exactly why we pair fundamental valuation with Stage 2 technical discipline. A $92.00 fundamental destination tells us what DFIN is worth over 12 to 18 months; the chart in Chapter 8 tells us when the risk-reward to reach it is actually in our favor.

book_subsections.title: 7F. Stress-Testing the Bear Case Multiple ($52.00 Downside Floor)
paragraphs: Before we leave valuation, let's stress-test the downside just as rigorously as the upside. What would it take for DFIN to trade down to our $52.00 Bear Case? Suppose high interest rates shut down US IPOs and M&A again in 2027, pushing Compliance and Communications Management down 10% and stalling Venue Virtual Data Rooms. Even in that harsh scenario, ActiveDisclosure and Arc Suite are recurring compliance subscriptions that keep Software Solutions generating over $370 million in sales. If consolidated Adjusted EBITDA dips toward $215 million and the market compresses DFIN back to 6.0 times EV-to-EBITDA—roughly a $1.49 billion enterprise value—subtracting $150 million of net debt across 24.5 million shares yields roughly $54.80, or $52.00 on a conservative Bear Case. Knowing that $52.00 floor helps us size our risk with precision.
